description: Isolation, idealisation and marital breakdown. Zaretsky's Marxist and Delphy and Leonard's feminist critiques.
content_html:
Why Are Families Criticised?

While functionalist sociologists emphasise the positive functions that families perform, a range of other perspectives offer sustained critiques of family life. These critiques come from different directions: feminist and Marxist sociologists identify structural problems with the family as an institution, while other critics point to the gap between the idealised image of family life and its lived reality. Understanding these criticisms — and the competing perspectives behind them — is central to the AQA families topic.

The Problem of Isolation

One criticism of the modern nuclear family is that it has become socially isolated. As the nuclear family has become more self-contained and home-centred (what Willmott and Young called “privatised”), it has lost contact with extended kinship networks and local communities. This isolation can place enormous pressure on individual family members, particularly when problems arise: there is no wider network to absorb the stress. Critics argue that the isolated nuclear family is an emotionally intense unit that can generate conflict, mental health problems and domestic violence, rather than automatically providing the “warm bath” effect that Parsons described.

Unrealistic Idealisation and Loss of Traditional Functions

A related criticism is the idealisation of family life. Advertising, popular culture and political discourse consistently portray the family as a place of unconditional love and support. Critics argue that this idealised image conceals the very real conflicts, inequalities and abuses that occur within families. Domestic violence, emotional abuse, child neglect and financial exploitation are all more likely to occur within family settings than between strangers — yet these realities are underrepresented in public discourse about family life.

Sociologists also note the loss of traditional functions from the family. Functions once performed within the family — economic production, religious instruction, health care, education — have been transferred to external institutions (schools, hospitals, the state, employers). Parsons acknowledged this and argued that the family adapted by specialising in primary socialisation and personality stabilisation. Critics, however, argue that this “loss of functions” has left some families without a clear sense of purpose and has reduced the family’s capacity to support its members in practical ways.

Dysfunctional families are those in which relationships cause harm rather than provide support. Sociologists use the term to describe families characterised by persistent conflict, domestic violence, substance abuse, neglect or emotional harm. The New Right argues that growing family diversity — particularly the growth of lone parent families and cohabitation — has increased the prevalence of dysfunctional families and associated social problems. Feminist sociologists challenge this, arguing that the concept of “dysfunctional family” is often used to pathologise lone parent families without recognising the structural causes of their difficulties (poverty, lack of affordable child care, the gender pay gap).

Marital breakdown is a related concern. This can take the form of legal divorce, long-term separation, or an empty shell marriage — a marriage that continues legally but in which the partners have effectively ceased to have a meaningful relationship. Sociologists distinguish between marital breakdown and divorce: not all unhappy marriages end in divorce, and not all divorces indicate relationship failure (some reflect changing legal and social norms).

The Status and Role of Women Within Families: Feminist Critiques

Feminist sociologists have been among the most influential critics of the family as an institution. Rather than viewing the family as a haven, they identify it as a site of patriarchy. Two key feminist accounts are particularly important for the AQA specification.

Ann Oakley argued that the role of women within families has been constructed around the expectation of unpaid domestic service. Women’s labour in the home — cooking, cleaning, child care, emotional management — is treated as natural and invisible rather than as skilled work with economic value. The conventional family, Oakley argued, is not a partnership of equals but a system in which women’s time and labour are taken for granted.

Delphy and Leonard developed a more explicitly structural feminist critique in their work. They argued that the family is best understood as a patriarchal family — an economic institution in which the husband is the head and the primary beneficiary of all the work performed within the household. Delphy and Leonard argued that women’s domestic labour is a form of economic exploitation: women produce services and care for which they receive little or no financial compensation. This is not a matter of individual men being selfish but of a structural arrangement in which men as a group systematically benefit from women’s unpaid work in the family.

Key Fact

Two major critical perspectives on the family are: Zaretsky’s Marxist critique (the family serves capitalism by reproducing the labour force and absorbing worker discontent) and Delphy and Leonard’s feminist critique (the family is a patriarchal economic institution in which women’s domestic labour is exploited for men’s benefit).

Zaretsky’s Marxist Critique

Eli Zaretsky (1976) offered a Marxist account of the development of the family under capitalism. He argued that as industrial capitalism separated work from home in the nineteenth century, the family came to be presented as a private refuge from the public world of economic exploitation. But Zaretsky argued that this was an ideological function: the family does not actually provide freedom from capitalism but instead naturalises and reproduces capitalist social relations. Workers who experience alienation and exploitation at work are directed to seek fulfilment in family life — reducing the likelihood of collective resistance to capitalism.

Zaretsky also argued that the family functions as a unit of consumption, purchasing the commodities produced by capitalist industry. The home — filled with appliances, food, clothing and entertainment — is a major market for capitalist goods. From this perspective, the celebration of home and family life in consumer culture serves the interests of the bourgeoisie rather than genuinely meeting workers’ needs.

Key Fact

Delphy and Leonard argued the family is a patriarchal economic institution exploiting women’s unpaid labour. Zaretsky argued the family serves capitalism by absorbing worker discontent and acting as a unit of consumption.

Functionalists respond to these criticisms by arguing that critics focus on the dysfunctions of family life while undervaluing its genuine benefits. Murdock and Parsons maintained that the family performs necessary functions — particularly primary socialisation and personality stabilisation — that no other institution performs as effectively. While dysfunctional families clearly exist, functionalists argue that these represent failures of the institution rather than evidence against the institution itself. Parsons acknowledged that the isolated nuclear family could be emotionally intense, but argued that this intensity was the price of the deep emotional bonds that make effective primary socialisation possible.
exam_tip_html: On a 4-mark Describe question about Zaretsky or Delphy and Leonard, always name the sociologist and state both their general argument AND a specific mechanism. For Zaretsky: (1) the family absorbs worker discontent (keeping capitalism stable) and (2) acts as a unit of consumption (benefiting the bourgeoisie). For Delphy and Leonard: (1) the family is a patriarchal economic institution and (2) women’s domestic labour is exploited for men’s benefit. Describing only one mechanism usually earns 2 marks; both mechanisms with the sociologist named earns 4. On the 12-mark Discuss about criticisms of families, present the feminist critique (Oakley; Delphy and Leonard), the Marxist critique (Zaretsky) and the functionalist defence (Murdock, Parsons) as three competing perspectives, then reach a supported judgement.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Criticisms of families include: social isolation of the nuclear family; unrealistic idealisation concealing conflict and abuse; loss of traditional functions; dysfunctional families; marital breakdown; empty shell marriages; and the inferior status and role of women within families.
  • Delphy and Leonard's feminist critique identifies the family as a patriarchal economic institution in which women's domestic labour is systematically exploited for men's benefit. Oakley argued that women's role as homemaker is not complementary but exploitative.
  • Zaretsky's Marxist critique argues that the family serves capitalism by absorbing worker discontent (reducing resistance) and functioning as a unit of consumption (generating profit for the bourgeoisie). Both critiques challenge the functionalist view that the family benefits all members equally.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes Zaretsky's Marxist view of the family?
A) The family is a positive institution that performs essential functions for society
B) The family serves capitalism by reproducing the labour force and absorbing worker discontent
C) The family has become more equal as women have entered paid employment
D) The family performs primary socialisation and stabilises adult personalities
practice_questions.marks: B) The family serves capitalism by reproducing the labour force and absorbing worker discontent [1 mark]

1 mark for indicating that the marriage continues legally; 1 mark for indicating that the emotional relationship between partners has effectively ended. Example: 'An empty shell marriage is one that continues legally but in which the partners have ceased to have a meaningful emotional relationship with each other.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one feminist criticism of the role and status of women within families.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a feminist criticism (e.g. women's domestic labour is exploited; the family is patriarchal; women perform the double shift; the conventional family disguises gender inequality). 2 marks for a developed description naming a feminist sociologist: e.g. 'Delphy and Leonard argued that the family is a patriarchal economic institution in which the husband is the chief beneficiary of all work performed within the household. Women's domestic labour — cooking, child care, emotional management — is appropriated for men's benefit, representing a form of systematic economic exploitation.'

practice_questions.text: Describe the key ideas of Delphy and Leonard on the feminist critique of families.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for naming Delphy and Leonard. 1 mark for identifying their general argument (the family is a patriarchal economic institution). 1 mark for describing the mechanism of exploitation: women's domestic labour (cooking, cleaning, child care, emotional support) is performed for the benefit of the husband/male partner. 1 mark for a developed point: e.g. Delphy and Leonard argued this is not about individual men's attitudes but a structural arrangement in which men as a class systematically benefit from women's unpaid work, making the family an institution of gender inequality rather than mutual support.

practice_questions.text: Describe the criticism that the nuclear family has become socially isolated.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying isolation as a criticism (the nuclear family has lost contact with wider kinship and community networks). 2 marks for a developed description: e.g. 'As the nuclear family became more privatised and home-centred (following the principle of stratified diffusion described by Willmott and Young), it lost the external support of extended kinship networks. This places intense pressure on individual family members — particularly during crises — and critics argue that isolated families are more vulnerable to conflict, domestic abuse and mental health problems, rather than automatically providing the "warm bath" of emotional support that Parsons described.'

practice_questions.text: "The family is a harmful institution for women." How far would sociologists agree with this view?
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists Would Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): A sustained two-sided argument. Arguments in support: Feminist view — Oakley argued the conventional family is based on women's unpaid domestic labour; Delphy and Leonard argued the family is a patriarchal economic institution exploiting women; the double shift adds domestic labour to women's paid work; women are more likely to be victims of domestic violence in family settings. Arguments against: Functionalist view — Murdock argued the family performs essential positive functions for all members; Parsons's warm bath theory suggests the family supports both partners. Willmott and Young's march of progress suggests the family has become more equal over time. New Right perspective argues family diversity — not the traditional family — is the source of social problems. At least two named sociologists developed in detail. Sociological vocabulary used accurately (patriarchy, domestic division of labour, double shift, exploitation, primary socialisation). Supported conclusion.

Secure (7–9 marks): Both sides present, named sociologists referenced, judgement present.

Developing (4–6 marks): Relevant points, mainly one-sided or undeveloped.

Emerging (1–3 marks): Basic points, mainly description, little judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: Which sociologists developed a feminist critique arguing that the family is a patriarchal economic institution that exploits women's domestic labour?
Zaretsky argued that the family serves capitalism partly by acting as a unit of _____, purchasing goods that generate profit for the bourgeoisie.
A marriage that continues legally but in which the emotional relationship between partners has effectively ended is called an _____ marriage.
Delphy and Leonard argued that the family is a _____ economic institution in which women's domestic labour is exploited for men's benefit.
Match each sociologist to their criticism of the family:
right: The family serves capitalism by absorbing worker discontent and reproducing the workforce
The family is a patriarchal economic institution — women's labour is exploited for the husband's benefit
Women in paid employment still perform the majority of domestic tasks — the double shift

glossary_terms.definition: The process of presenting the family in an unrealistically positive light, emphasising love and harmony while concealing conflict, abuse and inequality.
In the context of the nuclear family, the condition of being cut off from wider kinship and community networks, leaving family members without external support.
A family in which relationships are characterised by persistent conflict, abuse, neglect or other serious dysfunction that harms rather than supports family members.
A marriage that continues legally but in which the emotional relationship between partners has effectively ended.
A system in which men hold structural power and women are systematically disadvantaged across social institutions including the family.
Delphy and Leonard's term for a family structure in which the husband is the head and chief beneficiary, and women's labour is appropriated for his benefit.
In Marxist theory, the class that owns the means of production and employs others for profit.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the isolation critique of the nuclear family?
flashcard_questions.a: The nuclear family has become cut off from wider kinship networks, placing intense pressure on individual members without external support.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the idealisation critique of family life?
flashcard_questions.a: Popular culture presents families as loving and harmonious, concealing the conflict, abuse and inequality that frequently occur within them.

flashcard_questions.q: What is an empty shell marriage?
flashcard_questions.a: A marriage that continues legally but in which the emotional relationship between partners has effectively ended.
A family in which relationships cause persistent harm through conflict, abuse, neglect or other serious dysfunction.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Zaretsky's Marxist critique of the family?
flashcard_questions.a: The family absorbs worker discontent, reducing resistance to capitalism, and acts as a unit of consumption generating profit for the bourgeoisie.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Delphy and Leonard argue about the family as an economic institution?
flashcard_questions.a: The family is a patriarchal institution in which women's domestic labour is systematically exploited for men's benefit.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Oakley describe the status of women within the conventional family?
flashcard_questions.a: Women's domestic labour is treated as natural and invisible rather than as skilled work with economic value.

flashcard_questions.q: What is patriarchy in feminist sociology?
flashcard_questions.a: A system in which men hold structural power and women are systematically disadvantaged across social institutions.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the functionalist response to criticisms of the family?
flashcard_questions.a: Dysfunctional families are failures of the institution, not evidence against it; the family still performs irreplaceable primary socialisation.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did Zaretsky argue that the family presents an ideological function for capitalism?
flashcard_questions.a: Workers directed to seek fulfilment in family life are less likely to engage in collective resistance to capitalist exploitation.

hero_image_caption: Feminist and Marxist sociologists argue that families can conceal inequality and exploitation behind an idealised image.
